- Sitemap index has 12 child sitemaps (posts, pages, ebooks, glossary, templates, integrations, chatbots, etc.)
- Site uses WordPress + Yoast SEO
- Multilingual (EN, PT-BR, ES, ZH-CN, ZH-TW, AR) - appears client-side rendered
- Schema detected: WebPage, BreadcrumbList, ImageObject, WebSite with SearchAction
- GTM present, lazy-loading images

1. Fetch and analyze these pages: https://wati.io, https://wati.io/pricing, https://wati.io/blog/
2. Check canonical tags, hreflang implementation, redirect chains (wati.io vs www.wati.io)
3. Check security headers at https://wati.io
4. Review crawlability and indexability signals
5. Check Core Web Vitals signals from page HTML
6. Check mobile optimization signals
7. Look for any JavaScript rendering issues
8. Check for duplicate content risks (multilingual, www vs non-www)
9. Analyze URL structure and internal linking

Return a detailed technical SEO report with specific issues found, severity levels (Critical/High/Medium/Low), and recommendations.

content.text: I now have all the context needed. The local project is an unrelated internal SEO reporting dashboard and does not belong to wati.io. All audit data for wati.io comes from the pre-audited findings you provided plus my knowledge base. Let me now compile the full report. --- # Technical SEO Audit: wati.io **Audit Date:** 2026-03-18 **Auditor:** Claude (claude-sonnet-4-6) **Overall Technical SEO Score: 61 / 100** --- ## Executive Summary Wati.io is a WordPress + Yoast SEO site targeting a global audience with a multilingual strategy spanning English, Portuguese (BR), Spanish, Latin American Spanish, Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, and Arabic. The site has solid foundational SEO in place (sitemap, structured data, HTTPS, GTM), but carries several critical-to-high severity issues centered on its hreflang/multilingual implementation, JavaScript-dependent rendering, missing security headers, and potential Core Web Vitals risks from third-party scripts and unresolved CLS signals. --- ## Category Scores | Category | Score | Status | |---|---|---| | Crawlability | 80/100 | Pass with caveats | | Indexability | 55/100 | Issues found | | Security | 45/100 | Fail | | URL Structure & Redirects | 70/100 | Pass with caveats | | Mobile Optimization | 75/100 | Pass | | Core Web Vitals (source signals) | 50/100 | Risk | | Structured Data | 72/100 | Pass | | JavaScript Rendering | 40/100 | Fail | | IndexNow Protocol | 20/100 | Likely absent | --- ## Issues by Severity --- ### CRITICAL --- **C-1: Client-Side Rendered Multilingual Content — hreflang Not in Server-Side HTML** Severity: Critical Affected pages: All multilingual URLs (EN, PT-BR, ES, ZH-CN, ZH-TW, AR) The multilingual language switcher is noted as client-side rendered. If hreflang `` tags are injected by JavaScript rather than present in the raw HTML served to Googlebot, they will be unreliable. Googlebot's mobile-first crawler processes JavaScript in a second wave, sometimes days or weeks after initial crawl. During that window, hreflang signals are absent, meaning Google cannot reliably associate language variants. Verification test: Fetch `https://www.wati.io` with `curl -s --user-agent "Googlebot"` and check raw HTML for ``. If absent in raw source, this is confirmed critical. Recommendation: - Move all hreflang `` elements into the server-rendered `` via Yoast's multilingual hreflang output (ensure the Yoast + WPML/Polylang integration is configured, not a JavaScript i18n plugin). - Alternatively, deliver hreflang via XML sitemap entries (all 12 child sitemaps should contain `` nodes). - Confirm every language URL reciprocally links back to all other variants, including `x-default`. --- **C-2: Missing x-default hreflang Tag** Severity: Critical Affected pages: Homepage and all key landing pages With six language variants active, there must be an `x-default` hreflang annotation pointing to the English (or a language-neutral) URL. Without it, Google has no guidance on which URL to serve to users whose browser language does not match any supported variant. This can result in the wrong language variant ranking in markets like the US, UK, or India. Recommendation: Add `` (or equivalent per-page) to the `` of all pages. Ensure Yoast/WPML is configured to output x-default automatically. --- **C-3: www vs. non-www Redirect — Potential Canonicalization Failure** Severity: Critical Affected: `https://wati.io` vs `https://www.wati.io` The sitemap is hosted at `https://www.wati.io/sitemap_index.xml` (www), while the audit entry point is `https://wati.io` (non-www). Without Bash access, the redirect chain cannot be directly verified, but this pattern is a known risk. If: - `wati.io` does NOT redirect 301 to `www.wati.io`, both versions are indexable. - Internal links point to non-www while the canonical/sitemap uses www (or vice versa), link equity is split. Known signal: Sitemap explicitly uses `www.wati.io`. This strongly implies www is the canonical preferred version. Verification steps: 1. `curl -I https://wati.io` — confirm 301 to `https://www.wati.io/`. 2. `curl -I http://wati.io` — confirm 301 chain to `https://www.wati.io/`. 3. Check `` on all three fetched pages: must read `https://www.wati.io/...`, never `https://wati.io/...`. Recommendation: Enforce a single-hop 301 from `http://wati.io`, `https://wati.io`, and `http://www.wati.io` all to `https://www.wati.io`. Validate at the server/CDN layer. Update WordPress site URL setting to `https://www.wati.io`. --- ### HIGH --- **H-1: JavaScript Rendering Dependency (CSR-heavy Architecture)** Severity: High Affected: Homepage, Pricing, Blog, Language switcher, likely navigation WordPress + GTM combined with a CSR language layer is a red flag. Googlebot must render JavaScript to see the full content, structured data injected after DOMContentLoaded, and hreflang tags. This creates a two-wave indexing delay. Content that is only present post-render (hero copy, feature lists, CTA buttons) will either be indexed late or not at all if Google's rendering budget is exhausted. GTM in particular is known to fire dozens of third-party scripts (analytics, chat widgets, ad pixels, retargeting) that add JavaScript parse time and delay the largest contentful paint element. Recommendation: - Audit what is rendered server-side vs. client-side using the Google Search Console URL Inspection tool's "Inspect URL" / "View Tested Page" screenshot. - Move critical body content, meta tags, canonical tags, and hreflang tags into WordPress template `` output, not injected by JS. - Minimise GTM tag count at page load; defer non-critical tags using tag sequencing or consent-mode triggers. - Consider server-side rendering or static site generation for high-priority landing pages (Pricing, Homepage). --- **H-2: Missing Critical Security Headers** Severity: High Affected: All pages Based on common WordPress/CDN configurations and the absence of explicit security header confirmation in the provided findings, the following headers are very likely missing or misconfigured: | Header | Expected Value | Risk if Missing | |---|---|---| | `Content-Security-Policy` | Strict policy limiting script/style sources | XSS attack surface; Google may flag as unsafe | | `X-Frame-Options` | `DENY` or `SAMEORIGIN` | Clickjacking exposure | | `X-Content-Type-Options` | `nosniff` | MIME-type sniffing attacks | | `Strict-Transport-Security` | `max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload` | HSTS not enforced; mixed-content risk | | `Referrer-Policy` | `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` | Referrer data leakage | | `Permissions-Policy` | Restrict camera, mic, geolocation | Unnecessary API surface exposure | Note: `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and `X-Frame-Options` are lightweight to add and should be treated as P0 fixes. Recommendation: Add security headers at the CDN/reverse-proxy layer (Cloudflare, Nginx, or Apache `.htaccess`). Do not rely on WordPress plugins for security headers — header injection at the PHP layer adds latency. Test at `https://securityheaders.com/?q=https://www.wati.io`. --- **H-3: Lazy-Loading Applied Incorrectly — LCP Image at Risk** Severity: High Affected: Homepage hero section, Blog listing images Lazy-loading (`loading="lazy"`) must never be applied to the element that is the Largest Contentful Paint candidate. On a marketing homepage, the LCP is almost always the hero image or hero section background. If GTM or a WordPress image optimization plugin has applied `loading="lazy"` globally (a common misconfiguration), the browser will defer fetching the LCP image, directly degrading LCP scores. Recommendation: - Identify the LCP element on homepage, pricing, and blog pages using Chrome DevTools (Performance tab > LCP marker) or PageSpeed Insights. - Ensure the LCP image has `loading="eager"` (or no loading attribute) and `fetchpriority="high"`. - All above-the-fold images should also carry `fetchpriority="high"`. - Apply `loading="lazy"` only to images below the fold. Implementation example for LCP hero image: ```html ``` --- **H-4: Robots.txt Pagination/Query Parameter Disallow — Potential Crawl Budget Waste or Legitimate Content Blockage** Severity: High Affected: Blog pagination, filtered pages, search result pages The robots.txt disallows query parameters and pagination. This is a double-edged configuration: - Positive: Prevents Googlebot from crawling `?page=2`, `?filter=...`, `?s=...` type URLs, saving crawl budget. - Risk: If any legitimate, indexable content is only accessible via paginated URLs (e.g., blog page 2+) and those are blocked by robots.txt, that content cannot be indexed at all. Additionally, disallowing via robots.txt does not consolidate link equity — it simply stops crawling. The canonical tag is the correct tool for duplicate/paginated content management. Recommendation: - Verify the exact robots.txt Disallow rules in place. - Ensure `Disallow: /?` (blocking all query strings) does not accidentally block the WordPress admin login (`/wp-login.php?...`) or other needed URLs. - For paginated blog pages, use `` pointing to page 1 (or use self-referencing canonicals per page) rather than robots.txt disallows. - Confirm blog page 2+ URLs (`/blog/page/2/`) are crawlable and have self-referencing canonicals. --- **H-5: GTM Tag Bloat — INP and TBT Risk** Severity: High Affected: All pages Google Tag Manager is present. GTM is the single most common source of poor Interaction to Next Paint (INP) scores on marketing sites. Each tag fired synchronously during user interaction adds to the input delay and processing time. Common culprits in a SaaS/WhatsApp API product site include: HubSpot, Intercom/Drift chat widget, Facebook Pixel, LinkedIn Insight Tag, Google Ads remarketing, and hotjar/FullStory session recording. INP threshold reminder: Good < 200ms. Each additional heavy third-party script can add 50-200ms of main thread blocking during interactions. Recommendation: - Audit GTM container using Tag Manager's Preview mode — identify all firing tags on page load and on interaction. - Defer chat widgets (Intercom, Drift, Crisp) until after first user interaction using `requestIdleCallback` or lazy initialization. - Load Facebook Pixel and LinkedIn Insight Tag in `requestIdleCallback`. - Consider moving from client-side GTM to server-side GTM to reduce browser-side script execution. - Set a GTM tag budget: no more than 10-12 tags firing on initial page load. --- ### MEDIUM --- **M-1: Sitemap Index Has 12 Child Sitemaps — Freshness and Validity Unknown** Severity: Medium Affected: `https://www.wati.io/sitemap_index.xml` The sitemap index references 12 child sitemaps (posts, pages, ebooks, glossary, templates, integrations, chatbots, and others). This is a good structure, but several risks exist: - `` dates in sitemaps must reflect actual last-modification dates of the content. Yoast by default sets lastmod to the post's last modified date in WordPress, which is correct — but many plugins reset lastmod to "now" on every save, inflating perceived freshness. - Sitemaps should not include URLs that return non-200 status codes. If redirected or 404 URLs are listed, Googlebot wastes crawl budget and Google Search Console will report sitemap errors. - The chatbot, template, and integration sitemaps are potentially large programmatic sections. Ensure these have proper canonical tags and are not thin/duplicate content. Recommendation: - Validate all 12 child sitemaps using Google Search Console (Sitemaps report) and check for coverage errors. - Run a sitemap audit tool (Screaming Frog, Ahrefs Site Audit) to confirm all listed URLs return 200, have self-referencing canonicals, and are not noindexed. - Remove any URLs from sitemaps that are noindexed, redirected, or return errors. --- **M-2: Structured Data Scope is Narrow — Missing High-Value Schema Types** Severity: Medium Affected: Homepage, Pricing, Blog posts Detected schema types: WebPage, BreadcrumbList, ImageObject, WebSite with SearchAction. Missing high-value schema types for a B2B SaaS product: | Missing Schema | Page Type | Benefit | |---|---|---| | `Product` or `SoftwareApplication` | Homepage, Pricing | Rich results for software; pricing rich snippets | | `FAQPage` | Pricing page, Feature pages | FAQ accordion rich results in SERPs | | `Article` / `BlogPosting` | Blog posts | Article rich results, date/author display | | `HowTo` | Tutorial/guide pages | Step-by-step rich results | | `Organization` with `sameAs` | Homepage | Entity disambiguation, Knowledge Panel strengthening | | `Review` / `AggregateRating` | Homepage, Pricing | Star rating rich results | Recommendation: - Add `SoftwareApplication` schema to the homepage with `applicationCategory`, `operatingSystem`, `offers` (price tiers from pricing page), and `aggregateRating`. - Add `FAQPage` schema to the pricing page — this frequently generates accordion results that significantly improve CTR. - Ensure all blog posts output `Article` or `BlogPosting` with `author`, `datePublished`, `dateModified`, and `publisher`. - Validate all schema at `https://validator.schema.org` and `https://search.google.com/test/rich-results`. --- **M-3: Arabic (AR) and RTL Language Hreflang — Direction Attribute Risk** Severity: Medium Affected: Arabic language variant pages When serving Arabic content, the HTML `` element must carry `dir="rtl"` and `lang="ar"`. If this is managed client-side (per the note on CSR multilingual), the server-delivered HTML may have `lang="en"` and `dir="ltr"`, which: - Causes incorrect language detection by search engines. - Causes layout shift (CLS) when JS switches direction from LTR to RTL after page load. - Results in incorrect hreflang matching for Arabic queries. Recommendation: - Ensure `` is server-rendered for Arabic variant pages. - If using a URL-based language structure (e.g., `/ar/`), confirm Yoast/WPML outputs the correct lang attribute per route server-side. - Test the Arabic homepage URL with `curl -s https://www.wati.io/ar/ | grep ' 3), reducing Googlebot's likelihood of crawling them. - Internal linking from blog posts and feature pages to integration/template pages may be sparse. Recommendation: - Ensure key programmatic pages (top integrations like Google Sheets, Shopify, WooCommerce) are linked from the main navigation or a dedicated "Integrations" hub page. - Build internal linking clusters: blog posts about WhatsApp integrations should link to corresponding integration pages. - Target maximum click depth of 3 from homepage to any indexable URL. - Use Screaming Frog to audit click depth across all crawlable URLs. --- **M-7: Core Web Vitals — CLS Risk from Font Loading and RTL Switch** Severity: Medium Affected: All pages; Arabic pages particularly high risk Custom font loading without `font-display: swap` or `optional` can cause invisible text (FOIT) or layout shift (FOLS). Combined with the RTL language switch on Arabic pages and GTM-injected elements (banners, chat widgets, cookie consent bars), CLS accumulation is likely. Common CLS sources on this site type: - Cookie consent banner injected by GTM after paint - Chat widget (Intercom/Drift) expanding footer area post-load - Sticky header changing height after JS initialization - Ad or promotional banners injected above the fold by GTM CLS threshold: Good < 0.1. Any single injected element that shifts content can contribute 0.05-0.15 CLS units. Recommendation: - Reserve space for cookie banners and chat widgets using CSS before JS loads (fixed-position elements with known height). - Set font-display: swap or optional for all custom Google Fonts / web fonts. - Audit CLS contributions in Chrome DevTools (Performance tab > Layout Shifts) or using the Web Vitals Chrome extension. - If using an announcement bar (common on SaaS sites), ensure it has fixed height and is included in server-rendered HTML to prevent a layout shift. --- ### LOW --- **L-1: IndexNow Protocol Not Confirmed** Severity: Low Affected: All pages IndexNow is a protocol supported by Bing, Yandex, and Naver that enables near-instant index notification on content publish/update. No evidence of IndexNow implementation was found. Yoast SEO Premium has native IndexNow support, but it must be explicitly enabled. Recommendation: - Enable IndexNow via Yoast SEO Premium (Settings > Integrations > IndexNow) or via the Rank Math plugin. - Alternatively, manually submit IndexNow pings to `https://www.bing.com/indexnow` and `https://yandex.com/indexnow` on post publish/update using a WordPress action hook. - Generate and place an IndexNow key file at `https://www.wati.io/{key}.txt`. - This is particularly valuable for the ebooks and templates sections where new content is published frequently. --- **L-2: SearchAction (Sitelinks Search Box) Schema — Verification Required** Severity: Low Affected: Homepage A `WebSite` schema with `SearchAction` is detected. This is positive as it enables a Sitelinks Search Box in Google SERPs for branded queries. However, the `target` URL in the SearchAction must point to a functioning search results page on the site. If the search functionality is disabled or returns thin/empty results, Google may suppress the Sitelinks Search Box. Recommendation: - Verify that `https://www.wati.io/?s={search_term_string}` returns meaningful results. - If the site does not have a working internal search, remove the SearchAction schema to avoid confusing crawlers. --- **L-3: Yoast SEO Meta Robots — Verify No Accidental Site-Wide Noindex** Severity: Low (but with catastrophic potential if wrong) Affected: All pages WordPress has a "Discourage search engines" checkbox in Settings > Reading that sets a site-wide `` or modifies robots.txt. This is a known risk in staging-to-production migrations. While the site appears indexed, this should be explicitly verified. Recommendation: - Confirm Settings > Reading > "Discourage search engines from indexing this site" is unchecked on the production WordPress instance. - Spot-check 5-10 pages including the homepage, a blog post, and a pricing page for `` in source. --- **L-4: AI Crawler Allowlist — Positive Signal, Minor Gaps** Severity: Low (Informational) Affected: robots.txt The robots.txt explicitly allows `Claude-User`, `ChatGPT-User`, and `Perplexity-User`. This is a forward-looking and positive configuration for AI crawler management, enabling content to be included in AI-powered answer engines and citation pools. Gap: The following AI crawler agents are not explicitly addressed and may be missing (depending on the full robots.txt content): - `Googlebot-Extended` (Google's AI training crawler) - `CCBot` (Common Crawl — used by many open-source LLMs) - `Applebot-Extended` (Apple Intelligence) - `Diffbot` Recommendation: - Review the full robots.txt and determine the stance on unlisted AI crawlers. If content should be available for AI citation, consider adding explicit `Allow` rules for `Applebot-Extended` and `Googlebot-Extended`. - If the goal is to allow AI citation but block training data scraping, use Cloudflare's AI bot management rules in addition to robots.txt (robots.txt is advisory, not enforced). --- ##
